title: Async & the Event Loop
tagline: How JavaScript handles thousands of operations on a single thread

sections.content:
JavaScript is single-threaded yet powers servers handling millions of requests and UIs that stay buttery smooth. The secret is the **event loop** — a deceptively simple runtime mechanism that makes non-blocking I/O possible without spawning threads.

Understanding the event loop means understanding *exactly* when your code runs. It explains why `setTimeout(fn, 0)` doesn't execute immediately, why `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` runs before the next `setTimeout`, and why long synchronous loops freeze your UI. The execution model progresses from raw **callbacks** → **Promises** → **async/await**, each layer adding abstraction without changing the underlying event loop machinery.

sections.title: The Airport Gate Agent Analogy
sections.content:
Picture a single **gate agent** (the call stack) at an airport. Passengers (tasks) must be processed one at a time — no two passengers at the counter simultaneously.

When a passenger needs a boarding pass printed (I/O), the agent hands the request to the **printer room** (Web APIs / libuv) and takes the *next* passenger from the queue instead of standing idle. When the printer finishes, it puts a slip in the **urgent in-tray** (microtask queue) or the **regular queue** (macrotask queue).

The agent's rule: after each passenger, *empty the urgent in-tray completely* before touching the regular queue. This is why Promise callbacks (microtasks) always beat `setTimeout` callbacks (macrotasks) — the in-tray is always processed first, no matter how many slips pile up.

sections.title: Microtasks, Macrotasks, and the Execution Order
sections.content:
The event loop processes tasks in a strict order every **tick**:

1. **Execute the current synchronous code** on the call stack until empty.
2. **Drain the microtask queue completely** — every `Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, and `MutationObserver` callback, including any new microtasks enqueued during this phase.
3. **Execute one macrotask** from the macrotask queue — `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` (Node.js), I/O callbacks.
4. **Drain microtasks again** (from step 2).
5. Repeat from step 3.

**Microtasks**: `Promise.then/catch/finally`, `queueMicrotask()`, `async/await` resumptions. They are processed before the browser/runtime has a chance to render or run other I/O callbacks.

**Macrotasks**: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, I/O completion callbacks, UI events. Only one runs per loop iteration.

This ordering has real consequences: if you enqueue microtasks in a loop, you can **starve macrotasks** — including browser rendering. A recursive `Promise.resolve().then(...)` chain will block the UI just as surely as a synchronous `while(true)` loop.

**async/await** is syntactic sugar over Promises. `await expr` suspends the async function, returns control to the caller, and schedules the continuation as a microtask when `expr` resolves. No new threads are created — it is purely cooperative scheduling on the event loop.

sections.caption: Each event loop tick: sync code → drain all microtasks → one macrotask → repeat. Microtasks always run before the next macrotask.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The execution order confirms the rule: synchronous code runs first, then all microtasks (including ones enqueued during microtask execution), and only then the macrotask. `async/await` is shown as equivalent to chained `.then()` — identical event loop behavior, cleaner syntax.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Watch for microtask starvation:** if you create Promises in a tight loop that resolve immediately (e.g., `while(true) await Promise.resolve()`), you drain the microtask queue forever and the browser never renders a frame. For long-running iterative work, yield back to the macrotask queue with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` periodically to let the runtime breathe.

items: The **event loop** enables non-blocking I/O on a single thread: while the call stack is empty, it picks the next ready task from its queues.

**Microtasks** (`Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, `async/await` resumptions) run before **macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, I/O callbacks) — the entire microtask queue is drained before the next macrotask starts.
**async/await** is syntactic sugar over Promises; it does not create new threads and has identical event loop semantics to chained `.then()` calls.
Blocking the call stack with synchronous CPU work (large loops, `readFileSync`) starves the event loop and freezes I/O, UI rendering, and all other tasks.
**libuv** (Node.js) and browser Web APIs handle actual I/O asynchronously in native threads, posting completion callbacks back to the JS event loop — JS itself never blocks.

quiz.question: In what order does the event loop process the following: a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback (A) and a `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` callback (B) queued at the same time?
options: A then B — setTimeout was registered first
B then A — microtasks run before macrotasks
Simultaneously — the event loop runs them in parallel
A then B — setTimeout has higher priority
quiz.explanation: Promise.then callbacks are microtasks; setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks. The event loop drains ALL microtasks before executing any macrotask, so B always runs before A regardless of registration order.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a microtask source?
options: setTimeout
setInterval
Promise.then
setImmediate
quiz.explanation: `Promise.then/catch/finally` callbacks are microtasks. `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `setImmediate` (Node.js) all schedule macrotasks.

quiz.question: What does `await somePromise` do to the currently executing async function?
options: Creates a new OS thread to wait for the Promise
Blocks the entire JavaScript engine until the Promise resolves
Suspends the function and returns control to the event loop; the function resumes as a microtask when resolved
Converts the Promise to a synchronous value immediately
quiz.explanation: `await` suspends only the enclosing async function, not the entire engine. The event loop continues processing other tasks. When the awaited Promise resolves, the continuation is scheduled as a microtask.

quiz.question: Why does `fs.readFileSync('large.csv')` harm a Node.js HTTP server?
options: It causes a memory leak
It blocks the event loop, preventing all other requests from being handled during the read
Node.js does not support synchronous file reads
It creates too many OS threads
quiz.explanation: Synchronous I/O occupies the call stack for the entire duration. Since Node.js has one event loop thread, no other requests, timers, or callbacks can run until `readFileSync` returns.

quiz.question: What is the output of: `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`
options: A D C B
A B C D
A D B C
A C D B
quiz.explanation: Synchronous code runs first: A, then D. Then microtasks: C (Promise.then). Then macrotask: B (setTimeout 0). Result: A D C B.

quiz.question: libuv (used by Node.js) handles actual file I/O in:
options: The JavaScript event loop thread
The V8 garbage collector
A native thread pool, posting completion events back to the JS event loop
A separate Node.js process
quiz.explanation: libuv maintains a native thread pool (default 4 threads) for file system operations and other blocking OS calls. When complete, it posts a callback event to the JS event loop, which then runs the JS callback.

quiz.question: What risk does creating microtasks inside microtask handlers pose?
options: Stack overflow — microtasks use the call stack recursively
Microtask starvation — the macrotask queue and rendering are blocked indefinitely
Nothing — microtasks cannot enqueue other microtasks
Memory leaks — unreferenced Promises accumulate
quiz.explanation: The event loop drains ALL microtasks before any macrotask. If microtask handlers keep enqueuing new microtasks, the loop never reaches the macrotask queue — blocking timers, I/O callbacks, and browser rendering.

quiz.question: How does `async/await` relate to Promises under the hood?
options: async/await bypasses Promises and uses OS threads directly
async/await is syntactic sugar — the runtime transforms it into equivalent Promise.then chains
async/await is faster than Promises because it skips the microtask queue
async/await can only be used for network requests, not arbitrary Promises
quiz.explanation: The JS engine transforms `async/await` into Promise chains at a lower level. There is no performance difference and no new threading — `await` suspensions are scheduled as microtasks, identical to `.then()` continuations.

quiz.question: Which technique correctly yields control back to the event loop inside a long-running async loop to allow rendering?
options: Using synchronous `for` loop instead of `while`
Calling `clearTimeout()` periodically
`await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` to insert a macrotask checkpoint
Using `Promise.reject()` between iterations
quiz.explanation: `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))` suspends the async function and schedules its resumption as a macrotask (via setTimeout). This lets the event loop process UI events and renders between iterations.

quiz.question: In Node.js, which queue is processed AFTER all microtasks but BEFORE setTimeout callbacks?
options: The macrotask queue
The `setImmediate` check phase in the libuv event loop
There is no such queue — setTimeout runs immediately after microtasks
The promise rejection queue
quiz.explanation: Node.js's libuv event loop has phases: timers (setTimeout/setInterval), pending I/O, idle, poll, check (setImmediate), close callbacks. `setImmediate` callbacks run in the check phase, after I/O callbacks but the exact ordering vs setTimeout depends on context. Microtasks run between each phase.
